rule: Resting-HR baseline is the median of the last 60 days
summary: No study compares RHR baseline lengths. Overload-related RHR changes are small and can be masked by day-to-day noise, so a long, stable baseline is sensible; the downside is lag as aerobic fitness lowers RHR during the running ramp, which slightly biases the delta toward 'below baseline' (lenient). HRV-guided training meta-analysis found no RHR advantage, so RHR is a secondary signal; the 60-day number is a heuristic matched to the HRV window.

sources.note: Short-term overload raised resting HR (SMD 0.55); long-term overload showed no RHR change; small amplitude limits use
HRV-guided vs predefined training: no difference in resting HR (SMD 0.04) - RHR responds slowly/weakly
